utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Richard Ciaglinski who will be taken by Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Please could you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it's Richard Andrew Zbigniew Ciaglinski. The surname is Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could you spell your surname for us, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I will. C-i-a-g-l-i-n-s-k-i.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly pause between questions and answers for the sake of interpretation and the court reporter, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. As we will be speaking the same language, sir, we should try to keep a pause between question and answer. Thank you. Sir, did you give a statement to the ICTY in March 2000?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in November 2000, did you provide a short supplemental statement to the ICTY again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to review both of these statements recently?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And having reviewed these two statements, are you satisfied that they are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, both these statements have been combined under 65 ter 2488, and I would like to tender them into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statements will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And they would be assigned P00833 [sic], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you testify in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic before this Tribunal in April 2002?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And having reviewed the testimony, can you attest that you would provide substantially the same answers today if you were asked the same questions again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter 0289. And I would like to tender the testimony into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And finally, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00833, Your Honours. And I note 65 ter 2488 should reflect P00832.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, finally, did you testify in the trial of Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al. before this Tribunal in 2006?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And having done that, can you attest that you would give substantially the same answers today if you were asked the same questions again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Again I'll do my best, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter 05154. And I'd like to tender this transcript into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00834, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. The witness is a retired colonel in the British armed forces. He describes his commencement of operational duty with the OSCE/KVM in early December 1998. The witness was based in Pristina and his duties included organising and planning arms verification visits. He was able to conduct visits to VJ establishments and positions but had very limited access to the MUP sites. The role of arms and weapons verification was eventually abandoned as the verifiers were repeatedly denied access. The witness also had the role of chief liaison person for the KVM with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that's abbreviated FRY. The witness and other KVM officials met with the FRY authorities who were represented by the FRY Cooperation Commission. The FRY side was initially headed by General Dusan Loncar who regularly travelled to Belgrade. He was always called when information was required, and he would inform the OSCE when there was an incident to a member of the Serb forces. The witness describes Loncar's contacts and approval of higher authority in Belgrade particularly Nikola Sainovic. It was clear to the witness that Sainovic had the authority to speak on behalf of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are reading out a translation of a statement that the interpreters have been provided with, then that's fine, but otherwise I can see that there is a significant lag between what my learned friend is saying and the transcript itself, as well as the interpretation we are receiving. It's fine if the interpreters have been provided with the translation, but I can see that there's a discrepancy in terms of pace between the transcript and what Ms. Gopalan is reading out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for your concern, Mr. Djurdjic. You were reading fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I shall slow down, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't like asking counsel to slow down, but we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I most certainly will. The overall commander for the police in Kosovo was Lieutenant-General Sretan Lukic, but he refused to deal with the OSCE and left the job to Colonel Miroslav Mijatovic, who was the MUP representative on the Commission of Cooperation. The witness formed the impression that he was the second most senior MUP representative in Kosovo, and that Mijatovic was likely to have operational control of the MUP. In late February or March, 1999, special MUP forces arrived from outside Kosovo. The witness performed his duties until the withdrawal of the OSCE in March 1999. On 13 June, 1999, the witness re-entered Kosovo as a NATO officer. He was involved in ejecting the MUP from an office; and during this process, he witnessed MUP officers burning ID documents with Albanian names in a courtyard adjacent to the Ministry of Interior. And that's the end of the summary. I seem to be having some problems with my headphones. If I could just have a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, as you know, the Judges already have your statements and transcripts before them, and therefore I will only seek to highlight a few areas of your testimony, and your statements. Now, to begin with, sir, as your academic qualifications and military career are already set out in the statement, could you just briefly tell us whether you joined the British armed forces in 1974?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And are you still serving with the British armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, I retired four and a half years ago, and I now do work for the British government with British foreign office and I sort of go to conflict areas where I sort of take part in various aspects of conflict resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I'd like to move on to your time in Kosovo. Could you tell us when it was you went to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it was at the beginning of -- Kosovo -- we -- well, first of all, sorry, I'll go back. We arrived in a Skopje at the end of November, beginning of December, and then within a few days we moved across into Kosovo to Brezovica where there was a training centre where there was an induction course. And then a few days later, I moved into Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what year was this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And approximately when in 1998 did you arrive in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think it was the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And why did you go to Pristina at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Because I was put on to the staff of General Drewienkiewicz, known as DZ, who was the deputy -- one of the deputies of Ambassador Walker, and DZ was responsible for the -- he was chief of operations, so I was on the operation staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what organisation were you on the operation staff for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, initially, I understudied a lady called Donna Phelan from the American State Department, and she was responsible for weapons verification. She then moved on to become head of fusion, the intelligence information collection centre, and I took her job as head of verification.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in your statement you say that you went to Kosovo to be part of the British personnel on the KVM.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. Well, there was a British group that was sent. There were 114, 115 British personnel who went, but when I say "member of the British group" I think that's an error, because I was just -- it was an international staff. So I was just one of the many international staffs, but we were a British group that was sent to Kosovo which was then split up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what does KVM stand for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I understand correctly, these staff that you joined, that was headed by General DZ, was part of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the Kosovo Verification Mission or the KVM's mandate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, there were several. Obviously initially it was to carry out verification of the mandate that we were given, it was signed up by Slobodan -- President Slobodan Milosevic, and that was to verify that the sides had disengaged and that the Serbian side was keeping to the agreements and keeping the troops in barracks or heavy weapons were withdrawn and so on. And there were further mandates which was then to eventually run the elections but also there was a project to look at the legal system, the judiciary, the police, housing, and so on. So it was quite a wide mandate. But the initial one was to verify the state of play.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to the agreements that you referred to in a moment, but just taking a step back, the requirement that verification was to be conducted and that the sides had to be disengaged, so the -- one of the main tasks of the KVM, do you know why this was required at that time? What was the background that led up to necessitating such verification?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. Well, it does go back historically obviously, because leading up to the mission deploying, there are obviously -- everyone knows there was a great deal of fighting between the KLA and the Serbian side. The west was very unhappy with the situation, and NATO was very unhappy with the situation. And various threats were being made by NATO, NATO activation order had been signed which threatened to bomb Serbia. So I believe that around the May/June of 1998, President Milosevic and President Yeltsin met and there was agreed that some sort of mission would go in to just see what was going on to prove that everything was being done correctly. And that was known as an EU and -- European Union Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission. This preceded the KVM. And it was made up really of Defence attaches and others from Belgrade who went around Kosovo and sort of reported back on what they saw. So in about July of that year -- 6th of July, KDOM began its work. Then, as we know, the fighting intensified throughout the period and once again NATO got involved at making various threats. But, sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I just stop you there for a moment. When you refer to the KDOM are you referring to the Kosovo Diplomatic...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Observer Mission, yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And earlier on you mentioned the NATO activation order that was signed. If you recall, when was that order signed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I knew you were going to say that. I can't remember off the top of my head, no, I might have written it down somewhere. I know it was resigned in October. It was re-activated, second activation was given then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic is going to help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Two questions: First of all, I can see that we are now discussing the period during which the witness was not in Kosovo. Second of all, I see that the witness has an aide memoire or some notes before him, I don't know whether that is customary. In any case, he is now testifying about the period during which he was not in Kosovo and as well as wondering about his notes that he is using as reminders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Firstly, he is merely indicating the capacity in which he served and who it was that he succeeded, so I see no problem with that, Mr. Djurdjic. As for notes, Colonel, would you mind not referring to notes unless it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm very happy to do that it was just that there were so many dates there and although I followed the entire sort of procedure from back home when it was happening, it's difficult to remember exact dates and which UN Security Council instructions they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you need to verify from notes, would you publicly indicate that you would like to refer to your notes, and we can then decide whether that is appropriate. Carry on please, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, when we stopped off, we were discussing the second activation order from NATO. I think that is sufficient background in terms of the process that led up to the KVM being formed and your entry into Kosovo. But specifically, could you tell us what your role was within the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Of course. On arrival, I was working -- I was being trained for a few days at Brezovica and there was a possibility that I would remain in Brezovica as one of the trainers because of my background. And we were training the observers mainly initially in observation. And having been a Defence attache, I'm fairly well versed in the skills required to look at equipment, look at group formations, dispositions, and make some sort of assessment on it. But what happened is rather than staying at Brezovica, I was whisked away by General DZ; and within a few days of arriving in the headquarters in Pristina, I was told to start -- beginning to start working out a system of verifying what was in the agreement. In other words, to go around Kosovo, to see where the troops were, to see what weapons they had, to see what they were doing, to see if they had actually gone back to barracks. To visit the three company position that is were authorised by the agreement and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition to your role in verifying the arms, did you have another role that you played at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I certainly did. And that role initially was to be liaison officer to both sides from the KVM, from the headquarters, that was to be the liaison officer the KLA and to the commission which was based in Pristina. Which is like a second-level commission because there was a more -- a senior, higher level commission in Belgrade. So I would carry out both these meetings, but in fact it became very difficult for me to work on both sides because both sides became suspicious of my motives, and they wouldn't tell me things. I could just feel this wasn't a good idea; so I spoke to DZ and we appointed someone else to liaison with the KLA, and I just became liaison with the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify, when you refer to General DZ, I understand that's an abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, he was known as DZ because of his difficult name. Often I was known as CZ because of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What was his full name, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Karol Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe you referred to him in your statement. Now, you also speak about a commission that was set up in Pristina or at least based in Pristina. Is that the FRY Cooperation Commission that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct. We refer to it as the FRY Cooperation Commission, but we were very well aware that there was a senior level of that commission also in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this commission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was to deal with day-to-day problems, and passage of information in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In terms of membership in this commission, could you explain to us who the members were both on your side and the other side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. Well, on our side, I was not the senior member initially. General DZ or even Ambassador Walker or one of the deputy heads of mission would have been representing the KVM. I was always there with him, and there was also obviously an interpreter or two. And anyone else we needed to bring if there was a specific issue. That was the KVM side. On the other side, on the Serbian side, the commission in Pristina was headed by General Loncar, a retired general, whom I believed Mr. Walker had personally requested from Mr. Milosevic to be head of the commission. And Colonel Mijatovic from the MUP was normally there. More and more infrequently as time went on. And Colonel Kotur who was VJ officer. And on top of that, we had the odd people from -- who often changed, from Belgrade. I think there was a person called Mr. Babic now and again. And others who sort of came and went.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in relation to the verification duties that were carried out by the KVM, in general how successful was this process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I would say that the verification that we had planned was very unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And why would you say that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Because we weren't granted the access that we believe we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was the access that you believed you had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the agreements specifically said that we had freedom of moment and access throughout the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd now like to have a look at a number of agreements, some of which you have already referred to in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, may I provide the witness with a hard copy of these agreements just to ease the process of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter 00658, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, if you could go to tab 2 on your binder, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Second tab.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's labelled number 2.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just waiting for the document to appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's the original agreement between the OSCE and the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if we go to the last page of the agreement, we will see that it was signed by Bronislaw Geremek?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, Bronislaw Geremek.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who was Bronislaw Geremek at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: He was the Polish foreign minister who was the chairman in office of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this agreement between the OSCE and the FRY that we have before us, what function did it play in terms of the duties of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, this was our Bible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. And by that what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It means that we carried out our mission in accordance with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to take to a specific portion of this document. It is at the bottom of page 3, and it's section 3 that states begin "...specific terms of reference..." On e-court it begins on page 2 and moves on to page 3. Now, the specific terms of reference paragraph 1 which follows on to the next page, the last sentence reads: "Mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times." Colonel, could you comment on this section of the agreement, please? Was this term abided by?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. Well, as I said, this was the -- our raison d'etre from the beginning of the mission. This allowed us, this sentence gave us the authority to actually carry out our monitoring in the most effective way. And the way we interpreted it was that it's the freedom of access and movement was everywhere including barracks, garrisons, installations, police stations, whatever, in the whole of Kosovo. That was the idea. Unfortunately, we were often denied this freedom of access because of various activities of the MUP and the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And by various activities of the MUP and the VJ, what do you mean specifically?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, for example, if they declared an area to be an operational area or if they declared it to be a training area, they would seal off the entire countryside for miles around preventing us access to see what was actually happening inside. Similarly, they -- we had no authority -- they wouldn't allow us to enter any barracks even if we gave them prior notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in terms of countryside being sealed off and access being prevented, if you recall, is there a specific example that you had in mind where you were faced with this situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It often happened. I mean, I was being rung up on a daily basis by the regional centres. Your Honours, we had five regional centres that commanded areas of responsibility. And they would ring me up knowing that I had some access to Colonel Mijatovic or General Loncar or Colonel Kotur, and I maybe had some influence on allowing them to enter an area. So they would be ringing me virtually every day and saying, We can't get into a certain area, and we've heard there's been a shooting, a bombing, an artillery barrage whatever and we're not being allowed in, can you fix it? There were just so many, so many incidents of this. For example, when the training was going on near Podujevo, we couldn't enter the sort of air field area at all. We could just sit outside and see what was going on inside. When they were shelling villages in March near Vucitrn, again, we were prevented to enter. About the same time, another large exercise was going on in that area and both General DZ and I were held by a century of gun point who threatened to kill us if we insisted on entering the area. And that was until I rang General -- sorry, Colonel Kotur, and he cleared it, and we were allowed to go in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. And when you referred to the training in Podujevo, approximately what period of time did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That was -- it was the end of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And this incident where you were held at gunpoint, was this in the Vucitrn area as well, if I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this agreement into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00835, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to move on to another document but as it's a short while to the break, I wonder if I should proceed or whether it's best that I begin with the next document after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate with that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Certainly more than three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: By one or two minutes or a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would say about 5 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the break now. We will resume sitting at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness comes, I want to say something quickly, and you will tell me if it's possible or not. A large number of documents were admitted in the Milutinovic Defence case when this witness testified, 15 to 20 documents. I would like to make things brief and make a list of those exhibits used in Milosevic so that they are admitted into evidence here in our case, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this matter was raised in the Milutinovic case and there is a reference in the Milutinovic transcript where the Prosecutor provided the corresponding exhibit numbers for the Milutinovic documents in the -- sorry, for the Milosevic exhibit numbers in the Milutinovic case. So that information is already contained in the Milutinovic transcript. I am able to provide the corresponding Djordjevic 65 ter or exhibit numbers, if Your Honours would like, but from looking at the Milutinovic P numbers which are listed in the transcript, the process of conversion is fairly self-explanatory. I'm referring to page 6857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would be of assistance to ourselves and to Mr. Djurdjic if there was a table which cross-referenced the numbers, and if that is the case, we could, I believe, avoid the need during the evidence of the present witness, of having to tender documents that are on that list. We can deal with them when the witness is on his happy way home. So we will take up your suggestion, Mr. Djurdjic, but if it can be combined so that we see both the Milosevic and the Milutinovic numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree completely that all exhibits from the Milutinovic case admitted through this witness be admitted in the same way in our case, because if we admitted the transcript, it's normal that all these exhibits also be admitted. And the same criteria should apply to the Prosecution and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll leave that matter to counsel to prepare. Thank you. Sorry for that delay. We were acting in your interest as well as our own.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When we left off, sir, we were going to look at another document, and that is 65 ter 00395. That's the next tab on your binder. And while that is being called up on your screen, I'd just like to take you back to the answer that you gave in relation to the access issues we spoke about earlier. This is in relation to the shelling that took place in Vucitrn at the end of March. Could you tell us who was responsible for the shelling?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. Obviously the shelling was if it was artillery it would have been the VJ, but there was also a large number of MUP there who had armoured vehicles and they were using those.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when you say Vucitrn, are you refer to the municipality or are you referring to the town per se?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And for approximately how long did this shelling commence for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, that particular sort of action took nearly all day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And the day in question was somewhere in the late of March?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And were there other actions in that area, around that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was a very busy area, so there were -- there was often things on a smaller scale going on, but this was a large scale where the villages were being burned out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in terms of the shelling and the burning, were it the same forces that were responsible for both these activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: How do you mean? Do you mean the shelling and the burning?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Because initially you said that the shelling was VJ and supported by --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, usually the other way around. It was always the MUP who led on these activities with the VJ in support. The VJ usually providing some sort of outer cordon or providing the -- all the heavy equipment, or heavy artillery, whereas the actual ground forces were almost exclusively the MUP. So the burning would have been carried out and the attacks on the village would have been the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now going back to the document on the screen - and that's in tab 3 of what you have - do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, is this the Shaun Byrnes one, are we talking about the -- or the Clark-Naumann one? Sorry, 3, it's the Burns. I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is this agreement? What does it --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. This was an agreement that Shaun Byrnes who was the head of the United States Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission that he made with General Djordjevic about check-points. That was the main thrust of this document about the number of check-points and observation posts that there should be throughout the territory of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 1 of this document, I note that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Gopalan. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have all the same documents on the screen. This is not the document that the witness is talking about. I think he is being shown the wrong document. I have Clark-Naumann Agreement on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's my oversight. If I could call up the correct document now. And that would be 00394, please. My apologies. Now we have the correct document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And going back to paragraph 1, the first sentence refers to check-points that will be dismantled, whereas the second sentence refers to observation points. Could you explain what the difference is between these two terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Check-points were originally in place and these were physical barriers, physical obstructions, on the routes which impeded the movement of traffic and people. So the agreement was that these should be dismantled, removed, and instead replaced by observation posts which would be a grouping of MUP police, off the main route, close to the main route, so that they could actually observe the movement of personnel or traffic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And why was such a restriction required on the number of check-point or, in this case, observation points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the reason we asked for the check-points to be removed is because they were actually causing a great deal of hardship and difficulty for everyone in moving around Kosovo, and we believe the same could be established by having observation posts. And the observation posts could actually observe, and if they needed to, they could stop people as well, but they weren't physically blocking the roads and intimidating traffic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, and now going to the numbers that are set out in paragraph 1, there's a reference to 27 observation points on the lines of communication, and then a reference to one-third of these observation points being manned initially. Could you explain just a little bit about these numbers, the 27 and one-third. What did they mean on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, what we wanted to achieve was that 27 areas would have been designated as having observation posts. And you can see paragraph subparagraphs 1 to 5 below on the routes showing how many we thought would be a reasonable number, which was agreed by General Djordjevic. And there was no point in having all these manned because they were the same routes, so we believed it was sensible to just have no more than 9 of the 27 manned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in terms of the implementation of this section of the agreement, could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We became aware that this agreement was not actually being adhered to at all, and so I, in my role as verification man, I arranged a spot unannounced verification one day where we -- I sent out 40 teams of people onto the ground to each of the locations that we had identified that were being used as observation posts by the MUP, and we found that there were at least 27 of those occupied that day, not 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, I believe you referred to this spot-check in paragraph 1, page 3, of your statement for the Court's reference. And that this took place around February 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Were there other spot-checks that you conducted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We had -- this was the main spot-check carried out by me from the headquarters in Pristina, but the local areas, the regional centres, obviously kept a continuous record of how many of these check-points, sorry, observation posts were being manned. And that was the reason for this eventual spot-check and the report going off to the mission of cooperation, to point out to them that we had actually you know, caught them out. Because they were forever saying that they were sticking to the agreement, there were only 9 ever manned. But in fact as we discovered there were 27 at least that were manned that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What happened after this report was sent off to the Commission of Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this agreement into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if I could call up --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 00394, Your Honours, will be assigned P00836.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could call up 65 ter 00395, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, the agreement on the screen now, and that would be the next tab on your binder, that's tab 4. Do you recognise this agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. These are all agreements I carried with me all the time I was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is this agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is the -- it's referred to as the Clark-Naumann Agreement which was signed by Mr. Sainovic and General Djordjevic as a result of one of the NATO visits to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have to check if the interpretation is correct. I heard that these are the agreements that were made while I was in Kosovo as if the witness participated in this agreement and in its drafting. That's the interpretation that I received in B/C/S. I don't know what exactly is recorded in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we understand that the agreements were those carried by the witness during the time he was in Kosovo. Yes. He did not suggest that he was a negotiator or signatory, as I understand the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, you know exactly what is on the record. I only reacted to what I heard, and I wanted to make sure if what you have just said is on the record is correct, rather than what I heard, then it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, going back to the agreement, you said that it was called the Clark-Naumann Agreement? I have some questions for you about this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And it refers to a UN Security Council resolution 1199. Earlier in your testimony you were referring to UN Security Council resolution. Was this the resolution you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And moving on to the next page, paragraph 3. Just waiting for the document to appear on the screen. Paragraph 3 refers to police and Special Police and their normal peacetime activities. It also refers to heavy weapons and equipment remaining under MUP control in Kosovo and that they would be returned to cantonments and police stations. Now, this paragraph refers to the goals that the FRY authority had in mind when they announced these measures. Could you comment on the implementation of this paragraph in relation to the returning of heavy weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, the -- most of the -- of the equipment was put into the right places as was verified earlier on by the KDOM. But of course what happened then is that once KDOM had hand over its operations to the OSCE, KVM as was part of the agreement that KDOM would be absorbed into the KVM, we no longer seemed to have access to check any of these things. We were just told that that's where they are, that's what is happening. But of course we had no way of checking this because we couldn't enter any of the compounds or installations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When the reference is made to heavy weapons and equipment under MUP control, could you clarify for us if you know what sort of weapons are being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Anything I believe over 12.7 millimetres. So any sort of vehicle armament larger than 12.7 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Would this be within the regular range of weapons under MUP control?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the MUP certainly had weapons larger that than later on in March; they were using weapons larger than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, I'd now like to take you to paragraph 5 where reference is made to a number of locations. Now, early on in your testimony you've referred to some VJ garrisons. Were these the ones that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. We wouldn't call them garrisons. These were company groups which was agreed to, well never actually agreed eventually about the actual size of it, but Ambassador Walker had written a letter to Mr. Milosevic specifying what we believed was a reasonable size for a company group and that was roughly 10 tank -- up to 10 tanks and 120 personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the VJ, the paragraph above refers to additional VJ units and equipment that were brought after February 1998 into Kosovo being withdrawn. What was your experience in relation to that section of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, it certainly was withdrawn and the authorities were in compliance with that, but of course in March we found a huge influx of newer more modern and larger more powerful equipments being brought back in again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did this equipment belong solely to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, no. It was -- I mean, certainly the VJ wrought in new T-84 tanks and so on, but the MUP also brought in new armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00837, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, in response to some questions on this agreement, you mentioned that the KDOM had been absorbed into the KVM, if you recall, when was this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The absorption took place over a period of time. So some parts of the KDOM took longer to absorb than others. So, for example, the British element of the KDOM was absorbed really within the first part of December whereas the American part of KDOM, for example, the US Diplomatic Observe Mission I think went on or several months before it was fully absorbed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the additional vehicles that were brought in to Kosovo, what was the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Me and my photographs and also the observers from that regional centre near Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If you could clarify for us what it is that you saw in this area that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, the particular -- the particular train load of equipment I saw were T-84 tanks being brought in which are -- which was a step change from the type of equipment that used to be in Kosovo which was a T-55, for example. So we've gone from a 1950 type tank to a 1980s model which is a completely different animal.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when was it you saw this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This was again in March.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In March. Thank you. And in relation to the MUP, are you able to provide specific examples of what you saw in terms of what was brought in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I didn't actually personally see the equipment being brought in on trains that the MUP had, but the MUP had brought a lot of equipment in by road. And it was just, again, a complete new generation of armoured vehicle that were being brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in terms of time-frame, is it also in March?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The whole buildup was throughout March.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to another document, that's 00396, which is the next tab in your file. Sir, this document on the screen, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is the letter that Mr. Walker sent to Mr. Milosevic in response to all the agreements that we had trying to develop a base-line, if you like, of our operations and of what we -- the information we needed as to what was actually in Kosovo, which equipments were actually in Kosovo and the troop dispositions, troop numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And by "base-line" what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we had to -- in order to verify, carry out our verification mission that no new weapons were being brought in, we had to know what the start number was. And so this would have established, A, how many weapons that were actually in place, where they were; and also from trying to interpret the previous other agreements, what we regarded as heavy weapons, and what we regarded as check-points, observation post, what we thought company team was, what the size and composition and so on. So this was the base-line that was going to form our -- upon which our work would have been based for the remainder of our time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of this letter that was sent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Nothing. There was no response ever sent to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if that were the case, who did you conduct your verification tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We tried to -- we informed the Cooperation Commission that we would carry out our tasks in accordance with this letter, as we had nothing else to go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I see. Now, in this letter reference is also made to meetings -- Tuesday morning meetings, and this is at the bottom of page 2. It's the last sentence of page 2. It refers to a meetings on Tuesday morning. Now, did such meetings occur between the FRY liaison officers and members of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I believe that there might have been the odd meeting that took place in the KVM headquarters, but I believe that all this was superseded by our daily meetings we had at the Cooperation Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you tell us about these daily meetings, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, there was a daily planned coordination meeting that we held every day at 10.00 at which said General DZ would normally lead, but eventually I led these meetings. And I was to discuss any issue that is we might have, any problems we've had, any problems we received from the -- from our regional centres, any request we might have had, any passage of documentation, reports that we wanted to give to the Cooperation Commission. And in return, it was a chance for the Cooperation Commission to brief us as to what was going on, express their concerns or requests, passing it back to us. So, if they had a convoy coming in, they might wish to tell us about this convoy coming in so that we were aware of it. And we could take measures to make sure that it was running through the -- for the country-side safely.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how productive were these meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, they were very long. It wasn't unusual for the meetings to take five hours. Certainly in the early days of these meetings, maybe the first month, a lot of the meetings would have to do with the history of Kosovo. And once the Serbian side was happy that we all understood the history of Kosovo, then the meetings became a bit more productive. When I say productive, the meeting tended to be really an exchange of complaints. Colonel Mijatovic, if he was there, would usually rant and rave and shout at us telling us that we were responsible for his policemen being killed. There was also an argument about what the terminology for the KLA should be as terrorist, which we didn't dispute, but he wanted to argue it anyway. So sometimes they were not very productive, this is why they took five hours, and at times the information used to be delayed until the -- crucial information would be delayed until the end of the meeting when it could have been given to us at the beginning of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Why did you think that was the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know if it was to be deliberately difficult or maybe that was the way the procedures worked, but that's the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in terms of the frequency of these meetings over time, you mentioned that initially they took place on a daily basis. Was that the case throughout your time there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. As -- if we, for example, had -- if there was some activity, major activity going on in Kosovo earlier on in the mission, then obviously we had to have a follow-up meeting we would have another follow-up meeting the same day. If we needed to go into the field, if I had to go into the field with Colonel Kotur to look at something, we would do that as well. But as the mission progressed, and towards the March again when everything was kicking, starting up and kicking off, we could have several meetings in a day to try and resolve it. Around Christmas when we had the incident around Podujevo, again, you know, it was coming and going and several times to the Cooperation mission -- Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And during these meetings, did you raise issues in relation to the violation of the various agreements, was this a topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: All the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was the consequence of these complaints that you made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I mean at times thing did improve, I mean, for example, access, the limit of access to the areas when the VJ or MUP were deployed. This was a real bug there of ours, you know, if our people can't go in, they can't verify. Eventually, we -- a letter arrived from General Lazerovic saying to us that, well the letter said quite clearly, that the KVM would be allowed to go into those area, but in practice, somehow the information, this letter hadn't been disseminated to the units. And so when our people turned up in the field, they were still turned away. Then it really -- they would ring me, on my satellite phone, I would speak to one of the commission; if it was a MUP access problem, I would speak to Colonel Mijatovic. I passed the telephone to the guard of the company battalion commander who was there, he would be told to let us in, and we would go in. As soon as I left, ten minutes after me leaving, the situation reverted back to normal again and our people were denied access. So it was almost as if I was being allowed to go in, have a look, but others weren't necessarily -- well others were being obstructed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the MUP spot-check that you conducted earlier in the year, was this raised during a meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Oh yes, of course. Several times. And it was just, you know, accepted; and I think it was just pointed out that the situation demanded more observation points.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00838, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to some questions about the MUP's role in Kosovo. And you speak about this at page 9, paragraph 3, of your statement, and you say: "In my view, the primacy in Kosovo was with the MUP as they were responsible for the internal security problem. They led on all operations until a week or so before we withdrew." Now, could you explain to the Court how is it you formed this view on the role of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It was quite simple. The MUP were present everywhere, and any need to negotiate any incident that took place it was the MUP who were in command and in control. And the -- if the army was there, if the VJ were anywhere in sight, then they would be there as support. I believe this is fairly normal practice in an internal security situation where the police have primacy, and the military power is there to assist. However, you know, the situation had almost gone beyond what police would normally be expected to do, I believe. Whereas, you know, here you had the MUP actually fighting as infantry soldiers and behaving as infantry, and the VJ was purely there as a seconds line, if you like, with tanks and artillery, and heavy mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When you speak about the MUP being present everywhere, are you refer together the regular MUP or are you referring to some other MUP units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I mean, we were all aware that there was, well, there was several layers of MUP, of course. You know, you had the ordinary MUP policemen who you would see in Pristina towns, villages, you would see the ordinary traffic policemen occasionally. But then you, of course, you had the MUP who wore clothing similar to the military, combat kit, a camouflage kit; but of course it wasn't green, it was blue. And so, yes, I mean, that's why I was saying that they were everywhere. And of course there were different types of MUP also on top of that. So you had -- the MUP had been there for some time, you know, you had equipment which was fairly aged and the clothing, you know, can see was fairly old style. And then from the new year we noticed more and more, if you like, brand new MUP arriving with very nice uniforms, with new equipment, much more highly motivated, more disciplined, almost like elite Special Forces. So that was a sort of the final echelon of MUP, if you like, that arrived in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And this was sometime in the new year, you say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in terms of just general MUP activities that you referred to early on where you said the MUP was everywhere, did you witness any of these actions yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I'm trying to think. Usually I would arrive as the action was coming to an end or had finished. So I mean, I often saw the results of what had happened and the MUP was there. But for example, the incident in Podujevo, that was before Christmas, that was an incident where the MUP had tried to go in and sort of rescue a farmer and got involved in some very serious fighting. Yes, I was there for that, so I saw that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And as you've referred to the Podujevo incident a number of times, just to clarify, you've just mentioned an incident involving the farmer. Was there another incident that related to the access issue and the training-ground point that we spoke about earlier on in your testimony in the Podujevo area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I'm trying to refresh my memory. I mean, certainly in the Podujevo area, there was a tank positioned and the access was controlled to the area of -- to the west called Lapastica, Gornja Lapastica [indiscernible]. Again, access was very very difficult there, that was controlled completely by the VJ -- by the MUP. They were also guarding a tank that was up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That was all -- well, that particular position, the MUP position, was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. And so that would have been throughout the time --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Throughout the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- that you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please not overlap, and make a pause for the sake of the the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Apologies, we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to these operations, you also refer in your statement to joint operations between the VJ and the MUP. You say the army would supply the support, the fire-power, and set up the outer cordon. The police would be the ones that would then advance on KLA positions and villages. For the Court's reference, this is in page 9, paragraph 3? How did you come to form this view on how coordination operated between the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, for a start, even from our discussions in the mission, the Cooperation Commission, it was -- we were told that the VJ had no part to play in these activities. The primacy of security in Kosovo was the role of the MUP. And they were only being used -- the army would only be used if heavy support was require. So that was a statement actually from -- we heard many, many times, and it was seen, you know, that's the way the system operated. The police had primacy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did you see any of these joint operations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only like to ask my learned friend Ms. Gopalan to give me a reference in B/C/S, because I cannot find these passages in the statement to which she refers. And the witness just comments after her question and I cannot follow. That's one thing. I think it is the 2000 statement, that much is clear, but I cannot follow anything when she gives the number of the paragraph, first of all in my statement I have no paragraph numbers. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to improve your system of referencing, Ms. Gopalan, as you go along?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I can, Your Honours. Although the paragraphs are not numbered per se, my references to the paragraph numbers refer to the order in which they appear on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the page or in the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: On the page. On the page in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And I believe I've always indicated the page and the paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll see if this helps. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't matter now that my learned friend doesn't have it now. The pages do not coincide in our two versions. That's where the problem lies. But please go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to give the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Not at the moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would certainly assist for future reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will certainly ensure that in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will notice that Mr. Djurdjic is usually giving both English and B/C/S pages when he is doing it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When we stopped off, I was talking about paragraph 3 in page 9 and this was in relation to the joint operations conducted by the VJ and the MUP. And you finished off saying that the police had primacy. And I was just about to ask whether you actually witnessed any of this joint operations yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, for example, I mentioned it already. In the area in the municipality of Vucitrn to the south of the town of Vucitrn, when that large MUP operation was taking place against the villages to the west of their position, the army was there but in support. Sitting back, sort of waiting for a call to come forward if it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And this was the incident in Vucitrn that you said took place some time in March --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- early on. And you also spoke about an increasing number of MUP Special Forces coming in to Kosovo. Where is it that you observed this increase in Special Forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, wherever there was a new incident taking place, and we came across these people. I mean, it was very difficult to identify which unit they were from, because they almost always removed their unit identification badges.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when you say an increase in the number, are you able to provide an estimate as to the numbers in question that came in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, but it was just a greater number, obviously greater number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how were they different from the local MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I think I said already, that their clothing and their equipment -- their command structure seemed to be much more highly regimented and organised. So that they behaved very much like military units under command, very tough, very determined, very professional in what they were doing. By professional I mean that they knew what they were doing, they knew how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In terms of the command structure that you say was different or more professional, was this something that you observed from the general professionalism or was there a specific example that you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No, it was general professionalism. You could see that they were highly motivated, whereas the -- it was just the body postures, the -- their behaviour on the positions, their organisation, the way that they planned and sort of carried out the operation was much more military in style than previously when we had seen -- observed the MUP operation, you would quite often see the MUP just wandering up a hill towards a KLA position in the open. These people were quite different, they knew how to skirmish, they knew how to, sort of, behave as soldiers as opposed to policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you said that you would usually arrive -- arrive when an action was coming to an end or just about to finish. And that you saw the results of what had happened and that the MUP was there. What were the results that you saw as a result of these operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, one of our -- our main complaint was the -- it was the disproportionate use of force. That was our complaint all the time. There was no need to raze a whole village to the ground just because there might be some suspected KLA in the village. There was no need to -- at Rugovo, for example, when the minibus full of KLA was taken out, there was no need to fire 300 rounds and throw grenades into the back of the minibus to turn the people inside into slush. That was excessive. So this was the -- this was the normal problem. As I was saying, we tried to discuss, often discuss the meetings of the commission to try and bring about a degree of proportionality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And this incident in Rugovo that you talk about, when was this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That was December, I think around the 10th somewhere, just before Racak.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was the source of information in relation to this excessive use of force? How did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we went there and we saw it, and we have photographs of it. There were photographs taken. DZ was there personally, Walker was there, General Loncar was there, et cetera. So it was witnessed. I mean the actual scene was there for us to see and, of course, unfortunately, the scene we believe was also elaborated. People were taken out of the minibus and laid around the area to make it look as if there had been a major fire fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And were complaints of excessive use of force raised during the meetings you had with the Cooperation Commission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was the reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, that usually that you know it was a legitimate action and they were chasing down terrorists and what would we do in a similar situation. And I used to point out that we wouldn't do it that way. And I believe that Racak was finally a good example -- the funeral at Racak was a good example where we managed to persuade the authorities to scale down what they wanted to do. Initially they wanted to -- were basically informed that if they saw any terrorist at Racak funeral, they would attack immediately and get in there and take them out. So over a number of meetings, we persuaded them to do it a different way which, in fact, they did; and they did it very successfully, and they managed to pick up some of the terrorists after the funeral without causing any further incidents at the funeral. So it could be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you referred to Racak. What was it that happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I personally didn't go to Racak. I was in Kosovo, I was following up later on with the funeral arrangements and the bodies -- the repatriation of bodies with various negotiations to enter Racak village, but the world does know that 45 villages, people, Albanians, were killed at Racak.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who in the KVM was involved in visiting Racak? You mentioned you personally didn't go.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I didn't go. No. It was Ambassador Walker and General DZ were there for the first group to actually see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to another document. That's 00677, 65 ter number. And that would be the last document in your binder, sir. Waiting for it to come up on the page and in the English, I am looking at paragraph 1(a). The paragraph begins with: "Main areas of activity in Bukos ..." And follows on the third sentence says: "...this has changed the quality of such former exercise areas higher than usual levels of MUP VJ vehicle and weapon movement has been observed." Could you comment if this -- sorry, before I do that, let me just ask you a few questions about the document itself. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's a daily report published by the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And by the headquarter, which headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And were you involved in preparing such daily reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I had some input to them, yes. I didn't personally write them, but everyone be contributed to the input.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the sentence that I just referred to, "the higher than usual levels of MUP and VJ vehicles," was this consistent with your observations on the ground at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what is meant by this statement, could you explain to us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, with the larger number of vehicles and personnel, obviously the -- there are either more people in the -- more VJ and MUP in the territory, or they are preparing for some sort of activity, or they are sort of carrying out training. But there are certainly more, and if there are more people actually on the ground than the actual level of movement is restricted for the rest of the people. Ourselves and the local population.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. This update is dated 27th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And it covers the period for the day before. Does this date have any special significance or this time-period have any special significance in relation to the observation that we have just spoken about? The date is right at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Well, certainly there's a great deal more activity going on throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: At this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd now like to take you to the section headed "Security Situation Prizren District"?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: On the B/C/S that is on the same page, but we have to scroll down the B/C/S just a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: A few lines down, and that would be the third line from the bottom, there's a statement that reads: "EU AG observed several armed civilians." I'm interested in this reference to the armed civilians. Could you explain to us what this means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, we normally refer to armed civilians being Serbian armed civilians. We wouldn't refer to Albanian armed civilians, we would just refer to KLA usually because the only people armed in the -- amongst the Albanian side would have been the KLA; so armed civilians almost certainly refers to Serbian civilians. We did raise this issue at the commission, and we were basically told that in times of crisis it was normal to arm civilians because they had all -- they were all reservists anyway and they were trained and this was part of their duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did you have information on who armed these civilians or reservists?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we were told that they were just armed by the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how did you come to know this -- this arming of Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we discussed this again at the commission with Colonel Mijatovic and with the General Loncar and Kotur, and they would just explain to us that it was quite a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you actually see such armed civilians yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When did you start seeing them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: From about this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where in Kosovo did you see them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well we certainly -- I didn't see them in Pristina, for example. But certainly out in the country areas and the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you have in mind any specific villages, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I mean, almost everywhere we went we were seeing this. Not particularly, I mean I can't give you, I mean, I can name villages, but it would mean nothing. I saw them in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, I'm having some problems with my interpretation and headphones. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00839, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to move on to some other topics. In your statement, you referred to Nikola Sainovic and his activities in Kosovo and you provide some examples of his authority there. In your view, what was Sainovic's role in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I would say that he was a lynch pin. He was the conduit to which everyone reported in Kosovo. He was often in Kosovo.
