And I don't have personal knowledge that he spoke regularly on meetings with higher level in Belgrade, but from my point of view, I just saw that all the information, if anything had to be referred by the commission, they always said they had to refer it to Mr. Sainovic. And certainly from my experience, one of the meetings which I attended with Mr. Sainovic it was very apparent that he made things happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you often have the opportunity to meet with him, or was it just, as you say, at this meeting you referred to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic would normally meet with the Ambassador Keller who was one of our deputy heads of mission, a French ambassador. So that was a level of contact. So if we had problems at the border, border crossing from Macedonia, for example, into where we were detained for some reason, it was very easy that Keller would ring up Sainovic and the whole thing would be resolved in minutes. But I certainly had one meeting -- attended a meeting at which Mr. Sainovic presided.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Was this the meeting in Pristina that you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This was a meeting in Pristina. The meeting of cooperation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to provide any examples of his authority?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. For example, the day that -- going even back towards December when there was a possibility -- almost certain possibility likelihood of a battle between the Serbian side and the KLA, west of Podujevo, when I suggested that if I personally attended -- attempted to get the Serbian farmer out of KLA hands, would the MUP and the VJ hold back their attack until I had a go? And it was at that point that I was initially told that Loncar said he would contact Sainovic, and that he went next door and made a phone call, came back and said that it had been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know if Mr. Sainovic had authority over the MUP or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, he could certainly make decisions without counselling them about what could be done. For example, the example of Podujevo. But the meeting that Ambassador Keller would represented the OSCE at which Mr. Sainovic was presiding on the Serbian side, there were several examples there where he was able to make decisions, immediate decisions, as to, you know, what the outcomes are of in response to our requests. So, for example, I was allowed to go and see the prisoners in Nis, I was, you know, we were sort of told what would happen about helicopters, fuel; any issue at all that was raised, he was able to answer on the spot and give us guarantees that it was -- it would be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And how about Lieutenant-General Sretan Lukic, in your view what was his role in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, as far as I was concerned and as far as most people that I worked with were concerned, he was the boss of the MUP in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: How did you come to know this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we were told. And we could -- whenever Mijatovic had to refer to someone, he would defer to Lukic and, again, we were told at the cooperation mission [sic] that Lukic was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did Lukic attend any of the meetings with the Cooperation Commission that you had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: If he did, I can't remember. I'm not aware. It was almost always Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd now like to move on to another time-period. This is your departure from Kosovo, so sometime in March. If you could just clarify. When was it, if you remember, you left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: 20th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: 20th of March. And around this time, or after you left Kosovo, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We -- our whole KVM retired to Macedonia, and we moved to an area near the Ohrid Lake initially.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you go to a town in Macedonia called Blace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Blace?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Blace.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Probably. Many times. Sorry, I was there often.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: At this time period, did you go to such a place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 655, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You'll see a photograph appearing on the screen shortly, sir. Thank you. Sir, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I took it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where -- where is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This is just south of the border crossing, General Jankovic Blace and it's at the end -- it's where the railway line comes in from Kosovo into Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Probably within a few days of us arriving in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, it depicts fairly early stages of refugees arriving in Macedonia after they had been expelled, forcefully expelled from Kosovo. Unfortunately, the Macedonians wouldn't let them leave the field, so they had built up and built up until they were in the region of, we estimate, 25.000 people in an area of probably the size of four football fields.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When you say that they were expelled, do you know who expelled them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, what I did is -- this is one of my pictures I took, but I actually went down and I spoke to the people over several days in that field; and every one of them told me the same story that they had been rounded up from their houses, told to pack a bag, and get their bodies down to the railway station in Pristina where they were put onto trains. Prior to that, they had ID documents removed, all of their ID documents removed, put on the train. They had no idea where they were going. They then arrived several kilometres short of the border with Macedonia, were ordered off the train, and told to walk down the railway track. And that's how I first saw them, I just saw a long thin line of people carrying suitcases which is very reminiscent of what you might have seen if you were in the Holocaust.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the removal of their ID documents, did you learn why is it their documents were removed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, every one of them I spoke to told me the same story and that was that they were told they were having their -- any link with Kosovo removed so that they would not be able to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this photograph into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00840, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, just moving on on this issue of identity cards. I'd like to take you to the time that you re-entered Kosovo as a NATO officer sometime in June 1999. In your statement in the English you refer to -- sorry the correct reference is page 10, paragraph 4, of the English. You refer to MUP officers burning tens of thousands of document -- court documents in a courtyard adjacent to the MUP building. And that MUP officers were throwing documents from the windows. Could you elaborate more on what you saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in -- back in Kosovo, the main headquarters were set up just on the road out of Pristina towards the airport, but we were going to have a Cooperation Commission, if you like, headed by Brigadier-General Bailey, in one of the buildings actually in town. And the building that was selected was a building that wasn't the MUP police station, that was behind -- the MUP headquarters was behind these building. These were administrative buildings fronting the main road. And we moved into that building and we noticed that the -- the police were very busy emptying the building and throwing out whole boxes, files, through the window into a little courtyard sort of like a little nook in between the buildings, which they were burning. We were very, sort of, aware of this because the whole building as a result of this burning was full of smoke and it was, you know, pervading -- it was -- you have difficulty breathing. So we actually went down and had a look eventually at this fire, and I took out handfuls of documents and discovered that these were ID documents of various types.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Who did these ID documents belong to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, the B/C/S of this paragraph would be the fourth from the bottom of the last page before the witness acknowledgement, if it assists. Your Honours, I'd like your guidance on a matter. In the Milutinovic case, the witness had marked a document depicting what he has described to us now. I could either tender the document with the markings that he has made, or if Your Honours prefer, I can provide the witness with a clean copy to mark the document itself. I merely suggest this in the interest of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These markings were made in the course of the testimony in the earlier trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. These are in-court markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to assist. I fully agree with what Ms. Gopalan says since the witness did that during a hearing, it was admitted into evidence. It tallies with the proposal I made. I believe all such exhibits should be admitted in our case as well. If we admitted the whole transcript in the other case, then it will be logical to have that accompanied with the exhibits referring to it and then assign our respective Exhibit numbers. And Defence would like to have this practice accepted as well

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the marked document, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I call up the exhibit -- 65 ter number please on the screen. It's 05157.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And I will ask the witness to briefly explain his markings. Sir, this photograph before you, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what does it depicts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's a very nice picture of the car I was driving around Kosovo in, but behind the car is where the pile of burning papers is. The red markings on the top right-hand of the photograph show the window through which the papers are being thrown out. And you can just see this is taken several days later, but the fire is smouldering. You can see some of the smoke rising behind the vehicle. The reason I took the picture with the vehicle there was because I didn't want to be seen openly taking photographs of what I considered to be quite important evidence in front of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what about the red marking around your vehicle, what does that denote?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: That denotes the actual sort of size of the fire that was burning when we first arrived will.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where are these burning ID documents that you saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right behind the vehicle. They are behind the vehicle in that nook there between the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if you recall, how big was this pile?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: About the same size as my car is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00841, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in Pristina at this time, so in June, 1999, what did you -- what else did you witness in terms of the activities of the VJ or the MUP forces there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I mean, it's it probably didn't come as a huge surprise, but we were there -- I arrived on the very first day of the NATO arrival, and I was there throughout the first three weeks. And it took several days for the VJ and the MUP to pull out their forces. And the morale of the Serbian troops and the personnel was very high they were riding about leaving on the backs of all of their vehicles they could get their hands on, but the disturbing part was that every vehicle was loaded with loot. Every vehicle was loaded to the top with all sorts of things, refrigerators, TVs, there were cars being taken out, driven out, just endless convoys of this type of equipment being taken out. So obviously looting had gone to a very large extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where were these vehicles heading?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Heading back to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And for how long did you witness this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: This went on for days, until all the Serbs had pulled out, probably five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, at this stage, this is all the questions I have for you. Before I sit down, Your Honours, there's one remaining in-court exhibit that the witness marked in the Milutinovic case as well which I would like to tender into evidence as I wasn't intending to ask the witness to remark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And that is 05156. And in the Milutinovic case, it was referred to at T-8626.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going to tell us anything about the markings?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes. It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or is the witness going to, or you just want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would just like to tender it, Your Honours. I can explain the markings for you, or I could call it up and have the witness explain it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's on the screen now, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Before I tender it then, sir, perhaps you could explain the markings on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier on, you asked me questions about Podujevo and the action that was going to take place there as a result of the Serbian farmer being kidnapped by the KLA. Meeting I had in the morning with General Loncar and the rest of the commission, right at the end of the meeting I was informed that the unit, the tank battalion which is marked with the X, the circle with the X inside it, which is an air field location near the Batlava reservoir, that unit and other units had been ordered to use force or every method at their disposal to recapture the captured farmer. And this is when I proposed that I would volunteer to go and get the farmer out if permission was given. The other circles, just to the west of Podujevo, you can -- top left-hand corner, that dark area is the village of Podujevo, town of Podujevo, and there are three circles there. The small circle on the right -- bottom right of that group is the position we referred to as "tank hill" that was a MUP position with a VJ tank on it which was a perfectly working tank. And it controlled -- that position was a hill so it overlooked the road to the right which is the main road -- the main resupply route, if you like, for the Serbian authorities. That road went straight to Serbia. That was how all the resupply and troop movements came in and out of Kosovo. The larger circle is the area of activity where the KLA were functioning. And right to the left is -- the circle on the left is a village of area the Gornja Lapastica which is where the actual farmer was eventually found that was being held.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00842, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. We could go for some 12 minutes before the next normal break, or we could break early and resume early, which is your preference, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could start right away, or if you want to have a break first, I'll start then -- well, let's take the break and then move on uninterrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it will be most practical for everybody if we have the break now. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00 and we'll go through to the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ciaglinski. Did I pronounce that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just to make sure that I was addressing you correctly. My name is Veljko Djurdjic member of the Defence team of the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic, with me is Ms. Marie O'Leary, also a member of the Defence team. I have a few questions for you. Given that we do not speak the same language, nonetheless I would ask you to wait for the end of interpretation before you start replying. The same goes for me as well, of course. First at the outset I'd like to clear up a few things that may have been matters of translation. First of all, am I right in saying that you were not a witness to or present to the signing of the agreements Geremek-Jovanovic and Clark-Naumann, Sainovic-Byrnes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: You are correct, I did not witness any of the signings personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Secondly, I think there may have been a misunderstanding as to the dates of the incident in Rugovo. I think it was the 29th of January, 1999, am I correct, rather than December 1998?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember exactly, but I thought it was pretty close to the -- to my incident on the 15th of December. But I haven't got my paperwork with me, so I can't argue the date with you, I'm sorry. But I think we all know which incident we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will show you some documents, and then we'll discuss it further. Another thing, you said you were not in Rogovo. However, the interpretation I received was that you said that there were some 300 shells fired at the minivan, or did you mean to say 300 bullets? What did you say exactly, could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: They were bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ciaglinski, reading your statements that you provided in the course of the proceedings, I wanted to clear one thing up. Your basic degree was in what field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: In mathematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you complete that course?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Sometime in the 1970s, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you've completed your math degree, did you work anywhere? Were you employed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I was, because I did a math degree and a teaching degree as well, so I was employed for one year in a school teaching mathematics before I joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see in your statement that in 1974 you enrolled at the academy in Sandhurst, I don't know whether I'm pronouncing that right, and that you were there until 1985? 1975, sorry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a full military academy in the UK as far as I understand. Could you explain this one year only, how can one graduate from the military academy in a year?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's quite simple, really. What happens in the British military is that the British military accepts graduates, people who have already spent three or four years at university sharpening their minds, and then they spend one year at Sandhurst where they do purely military training. Following Sandhurst, when you go to your unit, you are then sent on further courses, whether it's platoon commanders courses, infantry courses, engineering courses, or whatever, during your first few years after you graduated from Sandhurst; but this is how long the Sandhurst course takes, and this is how we churn out British officers. It seems to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I have no doubts about that. What is your specialty? What did you specialise in during that one year?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Are we talking about the one year at Sandhurst? We all do the same. Every cadet at Sandhurst trains as infantry cadet. So by the time we leave Sandhurst, we are fully qualified to work up to and including company level, so in other words, the ability to be able to command a company of 120, 130 men. But obviously as you -- on leaving Sandhurst you are not given a company, you are given a platoon, so you work your way up, but with your qualified to that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From your statement I see that in May 1975 you obtained a degree and probably assigned a platoon. What was your rank after the one year of academy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me how did you progress through the military ranks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, my specialism, because of my previous teaching, was -- I was in training. I was a trainer within the military, so I held a number of training appointments in the army. But I was always attached to a different type of unit, so my first three years I commanded a platoon in an infantry unit. Later on, I was posted to a Gurkha engineer unit in Hong Kong where I was with the Gurkhas responsible for all sorts of things, mainly do with working on the border, sending the Chinese back or the Vietnamese boat people back, capturing them as they came in. I went -- I did various junior college of division staff college, so there was staff training involved during this -- my career. I did a masters degree while I was in the army for one year which was in training design. I was later on sent to Poland as the military attache which is a part of the embassy staff. I also did a whole tour in Bulgaria as defence attache as well. So my career is varied, and one thing I can say having worked on training with units from artillery, engineers, aviation, tanks and having studied and worked alongside these people, I have a very good cross-section of all arms of the military and how they function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've shared a lot of information. However, I wanted to know what it was that you taught those soldiers. What were you training them in? What kind of training were you teaching?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, when -- when I was working, for example, with the infantry units, I was actually training my own platoon. So I was actually, you know, training my platoon in war fighting. That was for three years. Later on, as I progressed through the ranks, I was responsible for the training, for the design of training of all sorts of things, but to do with military. So whether it was to do with training helicopter pilots, training tank commanders, designing simulation and training systems for -- to enable the people to train. At one point - I didn't say - I was actually running a team of consultants who were responsible for all the training in the army. In Germany, I was responsible for training the 1st Armoured Division. So it was my job to make sure that they were fully trained in war fighting or whatever skills they required, so I would plan and organised and arrange the training for the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in the statement that your career was in terms of supporting training systems and intelligence activities. These intelligence activities, did they have to do with the training, or your work within the British army? Before you became an attache.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Some of my work, for example, in Hong Kong I was the unit intelligence officer for a time. In my work in Berlin, I was doing some intelligence work because Berlin at the time was occupied so we had Russians and others there, and so some my work was involved in intelligence in Berlin as well. And then later on, as you say, I became a defence attache which is an art of collecting information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998, as I see, you were deployed to the British staff or headquarters for support in Rhinedahalen, again, I apologise if mispronouncing it; in any case, in Germany. Could you tell me what that location is, what were your tasks, and what were the units that you were assigned to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Right. The Rhinedahalen is a home of two groupings. One is the United Kingdom support command which I was part of and their job is to support the 1st Armoured Division in Germany, and that's what I just mentioned to you. I was actually responsible for designing the training and securing training areas, et cetera, for that division. And the other unit within the Rhinedahalen is the -- was the headquarters of the allied rapid reaction corps which General Mike Jackson was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The other unit, was that a British or a NATO unit? The rapid reaction unit headed by General Jackson.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: General Jackson's unit was a NATO unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Therefore you were part of a NATO unit back in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No. I was part of the United Kingdom support command grouping, which was in the same compound but a different function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for misunderstanding what you said. You say that you saw there was a vacancy, if I understood properly, within the KVM, and it's British part. Was that a public open vacancy or were you recommended? How did you come to apply for that post with the KVM, and the OSCE, of course?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: The way the system worked was when the British government decided to send a contingent and seconded to the OSCE - when I said the British Army, it's not the MOD - it was the foreign office who actually requested the personnel and then requested that the MOD provide a certain number of serving military officers, because the foreign office also recruited a number of retired personnel as well. So the MOD then decided how many people were required at which rank and they sent out signals, messages, to various commands saying, We require so many people at a certain rank from your unit to go to Kosovo. And I happened to be on duty that night when the signal arrived -- a written document arrived saying we require one lieutenant-colonel to go to Kosovo. So rather than giving it to anybody else, I spoke to my boss and he said, Yes, I think you're the man to go; you can volunteer for it, if you like. Because I didn't, I personally didn't -- he didn't have to select me, could have selected somebody else, because there were a number of people probably in Rhinedahalen that would have probably liked to go on this mission. Maybe because it was late at night and I was there, so I was offered the chance to go. What happened then, the second part of your question, is that the -- all the names were submitted by the MOD to the foreign office. The foreign office then passed the names to Vienna. And the OSCE then tried to match the skill sets of the people they were looking at to the jobs that they had wanted to fill in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I may have misheard, but I think that year you were still a lieutenant-colonel; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just waiting for the interpreters to catch up, that's why I didn't answer your question so quickly. Correct, I was a lieutenant-colonel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Back in 1998, in Germany in Rhinedahalen, did you work on any intelligence tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The group numbering 115 British personnel, well, who were selected for the KVM OSCE mission, out of that number, how many of them were active duty officers and how many retired officers, military officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I believe the majority were serving officers. There probably were just a handful of retired officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were placed rather high in the hierarchy of the mission in Pristina, can you tell me how many US personnel were there in the KVM, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's hard to tell because they kept themselves much to themselves when they were part of the KDOM, the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, and some of them always remained in that sort of side, I believe. But I don't know. I mean, I think there were -- there seemed to be less of them than there were of us, so not more than 100, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When referring to the mission, I don't mean the attached KDOM members, UK and US personnel, but I have in mind those who went directly into the verification mission of the OSCE the same way you did. Do you know how many French personnel were there in the verification mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think there's a slight problem here, because the French, the British, the Americans all sent personnel who had already been selected to be part of the verification mission. Part of those contingent selected for the verification mission were sent immediately to Kosovo to be part of a -- of the the KDOMs, because we wanted to have a presence straightaway in Kosovo. So for example, the British sent a dozen people immediately on activation, but the remainder, there were, sort of, 80 then, sort of, arrived in slower time after having gone through training in Brezovica. But then within a few weeks all the 115 had become part of the KVM, those who had been in the KDOM had become KVM. So how many French were there? Probably also somewhere between 50 and 100. Somewhere -- somewhere there are the figures, because we published the actual state of the number of personnel in Kosovo on a daily weekly basis so somewhere these figures do exist telling you exactly how many personnel of each nation there were on a daily basis in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are correct. I simply wanted to know the number without the nation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I only had numbers and not the nations that they pertained to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many Italians were there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I think I'm going to give you the same answer every time, because I cannot tell you the exact numbers of each nation that were there without referring to some documents which I don't have, but they do exist in the system. But yes, there were Italians, there were Russians, there were Poles, there was there almost everybody that was represented, virtually everyone from the whole of the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct, there were; but I'm interested in it for a different thing, as to how many people were there from the different countries. The last thing I wanted to ask you about the numbers is this: What about the federal republic of Germany, how many verifiers did they provide?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Probably a similar number to the ones I've just been speaking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doesn't it seem to you that the greatest number of verifiers came from NATO member states, if you look at the total?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: It's possible that there was a reason for that, if that's the case. I mean, I'm not disputing it, but there were also quite a few Russians there, they were not part of NATO. But the reason for the very quick deployment of, if you like, NATO nations, is because they have professional standing armies. And so we could quite easily produce 100 personnel, 200 personnel to sends on the missions. As could the Americans, as could the Germans, as could the French, as could the Italians; so these personnel are there, and they're trained. The difficulty is that a lot of the other nations didn't provide people with military police experience, they provided civilians. And it's much more difficult choosing a civilian for a combat zone, A, because they might not be very keen to go there, and secondly, they might not have the skills to be able to survive in a combat zone. We had no idea if there was going to be accommodation, if we had to live in the field, what the conditions were of security and safety. So you can't expect a civilian person to be deployed, a young woman or young man straight from university, college, with no survival skills built in. No skills of recognising what tanks are. I mean, we came across civilians who if they saw a large vehicle, to them it was a tank. It didn't matter if it wasn't a tank, it was an armoured personnel carrier but they described it as a tank. So what I'm saying to you is that we were able -- the NATO nations, the major ones, had the personnel trained and ready to go on these types of missions. Maybe the other smaller nations didn't, and it took them longer to select suitable people that could survive the rigors of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see your point. But that's a matter of selection that is up to the person who decides. And who, by the way, decided on the selection, how many people would come from different countries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I believe, I mean I wasn't there, so this is hearsay, you'd have to ask General DZ when he comes, because he was actually in the -- in Vienna as part of the whole planning and setting-up process. But nations would have been asked to provide. From my experience, often what happens is that nations are asked to provide 100 people; they come back and say, Sorry we can only we can provide 10. So then we have to go back to another nation and say, Okay, we've asked you for so many, can you provide more? And this is almost certainly what happened in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Formally and legally speaking, I understood that you signed a contract on engagement with the OSCE; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I'm trying to rack my brain, but we probably had to sign some documents to say that we were going to be complying with the rules and regulations; health and safety of the OSCE; financial matters; security, in terms of internal security. But I don't actually remember if there was a contract; I can't remember. It might have just been part of the myriad of paper that we had to fill in and sign for inoculations, for experience, knowledge of the area, suitability for the task, and so on. But -- you'll probably produce a piece of paper showing my contract, but I haven't -- I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to lose my train of thought. What was your combat experience before Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Before Kosovo, the British Army had very little combat experience, current, except for Northern Ireland and for the Falklands war. I was not in Falkland, but I was in Ireland. I carried out a staff job in Ireland, so my combat experience was not great.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you become an international employee when you joined the OSCE? Or you continued to become a member of the British armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: We were seconded to the OSCE, so we were in the chain of command of the OSCE and therefore I took all my instructions from members of the OSCE and that's where my responsibilities lay. However, I was paid still by the British Ministry of Defence, and so I was still a British army soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. I'd like to know about the relationship between the OSCE and NATO at the time when you were a verifier.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, again, personally I had no contacts or connections with NATO. But I am aware, because I was present on a few occasions when, for example, General DZ would be on the phone to Wesley Clark because something serious had happened in Kosovo and NATO had found out and they wanted to know from DZ what the situation was. But there was no chain of command between NATO and the OSCE. The only other thing we had was in Kumanovo, as you know, we had what we call the KVM extraction force, and their job -- it was a military unit commanded by Brigadier-General David Montgomery, and his task was if worse came to worse and the KVM had to be extracted in safety because of the deteriorating situation in Kosovo, they could have assisted us to get out in one piece so -- and that was part of NATO as well. So yes, we had to keep in touch with them. And of course, we had the NATO air element, you know, which was part of the agreement as well, so there were observation -- NATO observation aircraft flying over Kosovo at regular intervals with which we had contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were highly placed official of the OSCE, and I would like to ask but the flow of information between NATO and the Kosovo Verification Mission, the exchange of information and data. As far as the intervention is concerned, I am happy that it never happened. And it is a big question whether it would have succeeded if it had.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat again that if anyone was communicating at that level, the most senior NATO officer in the OSCE would have been General DZ, but what discussions he had with Wes Clark and others, I really can't tell you. Can I just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Of course you can't tell me about their personal communications even if you had overheard them. But I'm interested in official communications: the information you were providing and documents you were sharing. The official exchange of information, nothing on the private level. And to be quite frank with you, I've seen on many occasions that you have been on standby. You were on standby, you interrupted the mission on several occasions in order to maintain other contacts. I'm interested in the institutional communication between NATO and OSCE.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean talking about me being on standby, but there would have been an official exchange of information at the higher level, so in other words, our reports which went daily to the OSCE in Vienna would have been disseminated to member states and a copy obviously would have gone to NATO. And also, nations individually and the, sort of, head of each national contingent would have been writing a report on the daily or weekly activities which he would have sent back to his own country. So probably in the case of the Brits, we would have been write -- DZ would have been writing a report on every night which went to Vienna. Similarly, he would occasionally write a report which went to the Ministry of Defence mainly dealing with what was happening to us, to the British military personnel in his -- under his care. Not command, care.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that means that the members of the mission also had communication and maintained contact with the country that sent them, did I understand this correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think it's standard procedure in every mission that takes place in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have that kind of experience, but I thought that the international employees were in the service of the organisation that employed them, but it can be that I'm wrong. Let me ask you this: When you were joining the verification mission of the OSCE, did you get an appointment to a particular position, or did someone else decide what you were going to do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Initially, I believe they wanted to appoint me as being responsible for the training of all the verifiers coming into Brezovica; but a lot of those jobs had been taken by the Italians already and they were very keen to keep them, and so DZ, who knew me, took me into the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was a little confused reading all the statements, not only yours but other statements as well, about the function you discharged. Before Brezovica, did you have any training outside of Brezovica as preparation for this verification mission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes. In the first place, as I mentioned, the army, British army has its personnel trained to a fairly high level, so you know, most of the functions of -- on an international mission would have been carried out without any additional training. But because this was a new mission area, we had several days of training in a location in the UK where we were given all the background -- or as much as we could get -- background information on the war, the history of Kosovo and Kosovo Polje, and all this type of stuff, the language, the way things happened in this part of the world. Then we had additional medical training. We had additional mine awareness training, and communications training, evacuation procedures. All this type of stuff was given to us before we went to Brezovica. And at Brezovica we had additional training.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not interested in anything save for the information you received about the war. Tell me, what kind of information did you receive about the war during that training?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, as I said, we were given the historical run-through, what had happened, what was going on, you know, casualties, equipments, personnel involved, reasons for it, levels of destruction, this type of stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would like you to explain that in greater detail. What kind of information did you carry into Kosovo that you received in Britain? What kind of destruction was going on, what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I think, if I remember correctly, we were basically shown a lot of the photographs and film footage that journalists and others had shot of Kosovo at the time. And we also had people that came from Kosovo, so we had Kosovar Albanians that came to talk to as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the information derived from the news and the media. In what form did you receive such information, did it include video footage and films?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What kind of communication did you have with the media, the foreign news crews that were present there from the UK, the US, Germany, and others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Can you clarify? Do you mean? During our training or once we got to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you got to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, I think pretty good communications with the press. I remember doing a few interviews with the British and American press while I was here. We had our own press office as, as you know, in Pristina, which was manned by both Serbs and Albanians to try and get a balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not mean the press conferences, I meant in terms of sharing information. Was it customary for media representatives to be used as sources of information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, we certainly had our own press and information section, so we had a press spokesman who made statements on behalf of the mission. But if the press came into the field and spoke to verifiers, they were -- it could be done, and we didn't prevent our members speaking to the press because they usually spoke the truth, so there was nothing to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that journalists tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I didn't say that the journalists spoke the truth, I said that the members usually spoke the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it must have been a misunderstanding. But, for instance, Batam Hadjiu [phoen] was also a journalist, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to what you said about having some information from Kosovar Albanians before you arrived. Did you have any information from Yugoslavs, because it was still the time of Yugoslavia, about what was going on in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Of course we did. We had input from our foreign office to try and make the balanced view from both sides, but we also -- not only did we have Albanians who came to talk us to, but we also had Serbs who came to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, I was just referring to your answer concerning training. You said you had talks with Kosovar Albanians, you did not mention members of any other ethnic communities from Yugoslavia, but you did mention them now. What was your official title when you went from Brezovica to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, within a very short time I became the head of verification -- head of verification, weapons verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was within the framework of the operations team of the KVM; correct? In addition to you when you say verification of weapons, I suppose that was part of the staff of General DZ. Were there any other deputies for other areas in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Well, of course there were. The operations department was the largest department of all of them at the time and DZ had a number of deputies. So for example the head of the fusion cell, the information cell, was one key player. The head of operations office, DZ was chief of operations, so we had a head of operations as well. I was responsible for planning the verification so throughout Kosovo in writing instructions on it, so if we were sending a -- carrying out a centralised verification planned for Kosovo, then I would plan it; but I was just one of the planners. It was a very coordinated, very integrated headquarters, so we all knew what we were doing; each person knew what the other person was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On the same position that you occupied -- on the same level that you occupied, was there anyone in charge of the MUP or the KLA who was not a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: How do you mean "in charge of the KLA"? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You say your responsibility was weapons verification and verification of equipment and materiel, I would say that that is the military area you, you were DZ's deputy for the Army of Yugoslavia. Similarly, was there anyone covering the MUP, or as I seem to understand from your statement, anyone covering the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD CIAGLINSKI
utterances.text: Yes, of course there was. So what we had was we had, for example, a section where they were responsible to liaising and contacting the working with the -- with the MUP. Then we had -- we didn't have a section for the KLA, but we had a liaison for the KLA; someone had to talk to them. So I mean, when I stop doing the -- well, I was doing the verification work, and I was doing the liaison work at the same time with the Serbian commission, so if you like, I was the link there, at my level. And there were higher levels, but they didn't usually take part in the discussions unless there was something very very serious or something gone badly wrong. I'm trying to think, there probably were also policemen because we had real policemen in the mission. So I think that combined with the police element and the military, DZ's element, there were people working together talking to the MUP. I know that there was a Swedish policeman and a retired American colonel called Guy Sands who were doing most of the liaison for most of the time with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we've run out of time. I take it you have further questions? No harm in trying, Mr. Djurdjic. We must adjourn now for the day, and we resume -- Monday is a United Nations holiday, so we resume on Tuesday, I am afraid. It is at -- we are the afternoon sitting, I believe, which will be 2.15. Sorry about that, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing, Your Honour is that if we go too far into next week I have commitments in places like Armenia which I have to get to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm confident that you will finish on Tuesday, and that will occur by fair means or foul.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
